\chapter{But, Or, Why}
\label{ch:it-unire}
\hlchaptermodality{32}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can set one statement against another, offer a choice, ask why and answer because, say when, and say what something is for.}

The chapter's last lesson gives the infinitive its first job in a sentence. Since Chapter 5 it has been this book's dictionary form and nothing else; per plus the plain infinitive puts it to work and introduces no new word.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ma]{ma — setting one thing against another}

\label{lesson:IT-C32-ma}



\begin{quote}
A new chapter. Five retrievals, then the word.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{Che buono!} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{che} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{quarto / quarta} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{quinto / quinta} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mezzogiorno, mezzanotte} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{ma} — \textbf{but}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Parlo italiano, ma non capisco bene.} \textbf{Prendo il caffè, ma non prendo lo zucchero.} \textbf{Sono d'accordo, ma …} — I agree, but …
\end{quote}

It sits between two statements and marks the second as pulling against the first. That is all it does, and it never changes.

This book could already put two statements side by side with \textbf{e}, \textquotedblleft{}and\textquotedblright{} — the written-accent lesson had to gloss it in order to contrast it with \emph{è} — and it had no way at all to set one statement against another. The whole of arguing, qualifying and hedging starts here.

Beginning an answer with a bare \textbf{Ma …} is extremely common in speech and lands somewhere near English \emph{well …} — a soft objection before you make it.

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin had \textbf{two} words for \textquotedblleft{}more\textquotedblright{}: \textbf{plūs} and \textbf{magis}. Italian kept both and gave them different lives.

\textbf{Plūs} became \textbf{più}, which you have owned since the farewells chapter, inside \textbf{a più tardi}, \textquotedblleft{}until more late\textquotedblright{} — later.

\textbf{Magis} became \textbf{ma}. A word meaning \emph{more} became a word meaning \emph{but}, by way of \emph{rather}: \emph{not this, more this}.

Every western Romance language did the same and split differently. Spanish has \emph{más} for \textquotedblleft{}more\textquotedblright{} and \emph{pero} for \textquotedblleft{}but\textquotedblright{}, keeping \emph{mas} only in old writing. French has \emph{plus} and \textbf{mais} — that \emph{mais} is \emph{magis} too, the same word as Italian \emph{ma}. Meanwhile Latin's own word for \textquotedblleft{}but\textquotedblright{}, \textbf{sed}, which Cicero could not write a page without, was kept by none of them.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ma}
  \item \emph{Prendo il caffè, ma non prendo lo zucchero.}
  \item \emph{Sono d'accordo, ma …}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}but\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Ma}}.) Which Latin word is it? (\emph{\textbf{Magis}}, \textquotedblleft{}more\textquotedblright{}.) Which word in this book comes from the OTHER Latin word for more? (\emph{\textbf{Più}}, in \emph{a più tardi} — Latin \emph{plūs}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[o]{o — or}

\label{lesson:IT-C32-o}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back, and four longer throws.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ma} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{penso che} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sesto / sesta} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{settimo / settima} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{i mesi} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{o} — \textbf{or}.
\end{quote}

One letter, and with it the commonest question an Italian bar asks:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Caffè o tè?} · \textbf{Acqua o vino?} · \textbf{Prima o dopo?}
\end{quote}

It also lays out alternatives, which is how Italian asks about a preference far more often than with a verb for \emph{prefer}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Prendi il caffè o il tè?} — Will you have the coffee or the tea?
\end{quote}

Every noun there came from the drinks lessons. The only missing piece was the single letter between them.

Before a word beginning with \emph{o}, Italian often writes \textbf{od}, exactly as \emph{a} becomes \emph{ad}. You will meet it in print and never have to produce it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{O} is Latin \textbf{aut}, and Latin was fussier than Italian is. It had \textbf{aut} for the exclusive or — \emph{this one or that one, not both} — and \textbf{vel} for the inclusive one. Italian kept only \emph{aut}, which is why an Italian \emph{o} is as ambiguous as an English \emph{or}.

What survives of the difference is \textbf{oppure}, \textquotedblleft{}or else\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{o} + \emph{pure}. \emph{Aut} also went into English whole, in \emph{aut Caesar aut nihil} — Caesar or nothing.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{o}
  \item \emph{Caffè o tè?}
  \item \emph{Acqua o vino?}
  \item \emph{Prendi il caffè o il tè?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}or\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{O}}.) Which Latin word is it? (\emph{\textbf{Aut}}.) What did Latin have that Italian lost? (\emph{\textbf{Vel}}, \textbf{the inclusive or} — \emph{oppure} is what is left of the difference.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[perché]{perché — why, and because}

\label{lesson:IT-C32-perche}



\begin{quote}
The chapter's middle lesson, and the one that closes a hole this book has had from its first page.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{o} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{chi} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ottavo / ottava} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nono / nona} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{le stagioni} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: one word, both jobs}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{perché} — \textbf{why?} \emph{(asking)} and \textbf{because} \emph{(answering)}.
\end{quote}

The same word, spelled the same way, does both:

\begin{quote}
— \textbf{Perché non prendi il caffè?} — Why aren't you having the coffee? — \textbf{Perché non mi piace.} — Because I don't like it.
\end{quote}

That exchange is the point of the lesson: question and answer open with the identical word, and an Italian hears no oddity in it. Spanish splits them — \emph{¿por qué?} asking, \emph{porque} answering — and Italian asks you to remember nothing.

This book has spent its whole length explaining \textbf{why} Italian words are shaped as they are, and until this line it had no way to let you say \emph{because}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Perché} is \textbf{per} + \textbf{ché}. \emph{Per} is \textquotedblleft{}for, through\textquotedblright{} — the same \emph{per} that is in English \emph{per cent}, \textquotedblleft{}for each hundred.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Ché} is the \textbf{che} of the last chapter, wearing an accent because it now carries the stress at the end of the word.

So \emph{perché} is literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{for what}\textquotedblright{} — which is how a question about a reason becomes a statement of one. English does the same with another preposition: \emph{what for?}

The accent is acute (\textbf{é}) rather than grave (\emph{è}), and it is compulsory: the stress falls at the end, \emph{per-KEH}, and Italian marks a final-stressed vowel in writing, as it does on \emph{caffè} and \emph{lunedì}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{perché}
  \item \emph{Perché non prendi il caffè?}
  \item \emph{Perché non mi piace.}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you ask \textquotedblleft{}why?\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Perché}}.) How do you say \textquotedblleft{}because\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Perché}} — the same word.) What is it made of? (\emph{\textbf{Per}} \textbf{+} \emph{\textbf{ché}}, \textquotedblleft{}for what\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[quando]{quando — when}

\label{lesson:IT-C32-quando}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back, and the far end of the book.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{perché} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{che cosa} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{decimo / decima} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{undicesimo} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{il padre, la madre} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{quando} — \textbf{when}.
\end{quote}

Like \emph{perché}, it does two jobs with one shape. It asks:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Quando lavori?} — When do you work? \textbf{Quando prendi il caffè?}
\end{quote}

and it joins, putting two events at the same moment:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Quando lavoro, prendo un caffè.} — When I work, I have a coffee. \textbf{Quando non capisco, non rispondo.} — When I don't understand, I don't answer.
\end{quote}

The joining half is the one that changes what you can build. Every sentence in this book so far has described a single situation. \emph{Quando} stacks two of them and says they belong together in time.

Italian will let the \emph{quando} clause go either first or second — \emph{prendo un caffè quando lavoro} is equally good — and when it goes first a comma follows it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Quando} is Latin \textbf{quandō}, and that is the whole story. The long \emph{ō} shortened, and nothing else happened to it in two thousand years.

That is rarer than it sounds. Almost every word in this book has been reshaped on its way from Latin: \emph{quaerere} became \emph{chiedere}, \emph{causa} became \emph{cosa}, \emph{nōn} split into \emph{no} and \emph{non}, \emph{magis} became \emph{ma}, \emph{oculum} became \emph{occhio}. \emph{Quandō} stayed almost unchanged. Spanish \emph{cuando}, Portuguese \emph{quando} and Romanian \emph{când} kept it too.

Note the \emph{qu-} here does \textbf{not} become \emph{chi-}. That change happened before a stressed \emph{e} — \emph{quaerere} $\to$ \emph{chiedere}, \emph{quī} $\to$ \emph{chi} — and \emph{quando}'s vowel is an \emph{a}, so the \emph{qu} stayed \emph{qu}, said \emph{kw}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{quando}
  \item \emph{Quando lavori?}
  \item \emph{Quando lavoro, prendo un caffè.}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}when\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Quando}}.) Both as a question and as a joiner? (\textbf{Yes} — one word.) Why did the \emph{qu-} not become \emph{chi-} here? (\textbf{That change needed a stressed} \emph{\textbf{e}}; \emph{quando} has an \emph{a}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[per + infinito]{per + infinitive — saying what something is for}

\label{lesson:IT-C32-per}



\begin{quote}
The chapter closes with a pattern rather than a word.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{quando} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{Che buono!} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{prima} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dopo} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{il fratello, la sorella} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the pattern}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{per} + \textbf{the infinitive} — \textbf{in order to, to, for -ing}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Sono a Roma per lavorare.} — I'm in Rome to work. \textbf{Prendo un caffè per aspettare.} — I'll have a coffee while I wait. \textbf{Aspetto per capire.} — I'm waiting in order to understand.
\end{quote}

\textbf{This lesson introduces no new word.} \emph{Per} arrived one lesson ago inside \emph{perché} — \textquotedblleft{}for what\textquotedblright{} — and every infinitive in those examples was taught between Chapters 5 and 20: \emph{lavorare}, \emph{aspettare}, \emph{capire}.

What is new is the \textbf{infinitive doing a job}. Since the first \emph{-are} verbs the infinitive has been this book's dictionary form — the name you look a verb up under, \emph{parlare}, \emph{abitare}, \emph{leggere}, \emph{capire} — and it has never appeared inside a sentence. Here it does.

Italian asks less of you here than English does. English needs \emph{to} before some verbs, \emph{for} plus \emph{-ing} after nouns, and \emph{in order to} when it is being careful. Italian uses \textbf{per} and the plain infinitive for all of them, and the infinitive does not change for who is doing it:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Marco è a Roma per lavorare.} — Marco is in Rome to work.
\end{quote}

Same \emph{per lavorare}, whoever the person is.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{per lavorare}
  \item \emph{Sono a Roma per lavorare.}
  \item \emph{Aspetto per capire.}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}in order to\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Per}} \textbf{plus the infinitive}.) Does the infinitive change with the person? (\textbf{No} — \emph{per lavorare}, always.) Where had you already met \emph{per}? (\textbf{Inside} \emph{\textbf{perché}}, one lesson ago.)
\end{tcolorbox}
